events.title: Trump signed Executive Order 14401 accelerating FDA review and access to psychedelic drugs for serious mental illness treatment.
events.summary: President Trump signed Executive Order 14401 on April 18, 2026, directing federal agencies to accelerate research, clinical trials, and FDA approval pathways for psychedelic drugs (including ibogaine) to treat serious mental illnesses and reduce suicide rates. The order allocates $50 million from HHS existing funds for state-federal collaboration, establishes Right to Try access for eligible patients, directs the Attorney General to expedite rescheduling of Schedule I substances that complete Phase 3 trials, and mandates data-sharing between HHS, FDA, VA, and private sector partners. The order cites a 37 percent increase in suicide rates from 2000–2018 and notes veteran suicide rates are twice the general population.
events.why_relevant: The order represents a significant shift in federal drug policy and mental health treatment access, potentially expanding treatment options for millions of Americans with serious mental illness and elevated suicide risk, including veterans.
events.basis: It is the policy of my Administration to accelerate innovative research models and appropriate drug approvals to increase access to psychedelic drugs that could save lives and reverse the crisis of serious mental illness in America.

events.title: US Congress passes 10-day extension of Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act section 702
events.summary: Both chambers of Congress voted on April 18 to pass a brief 10-day extension of section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), a warrantless surveillance law, after Republican infighting blocked attempts at a longer reauthorization. The law allows national security agencies to collect texts and emails sent to and from foreigners outside the US without a warrant, with Americans' communications potentially swept up incidentally. A rare coalition of progressive Democrats and hardline Republicans opposed an unchanged extension, demanding a warrant requirement for Americans' communications. The House vote occurred after midnight following two failed procedural votes.
events.why_relevant: The extension perpetuates warrantless surveillance of Americans' communications without addressing privacy protections, maintaining a legal structure that enables mass collection without judicial oversight or warrant requirements.
events.basis: Both chambers of Congress voted in quick succession on Friday to pass a brief 10-day extension of a controversial warrantless surveillance law after Republican infighting tanked plans for a much longer renewal of the law with no changes.

events.title: House failed to extend FISA Section 702 without reform
events.summary: The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) of 1978 was scheduled to expire on April 20. Trump and Republican loyalists sought a simple renewal, but members of both parties opposed extending Section 702—which allows warrantless collection of communications data on foreigners but increasingly collects data on Americans—without reforms. Republican leaders attempted a five-year extension just after midnight Friday, but four Democrats and twelve Republicans voted against it, defeating the measure by 20 votes.
events.why_relevant: Bipartisan rejection of warrantless surveillance authority represents congressional resistance to executive power expansion and defense of privacy rights.
events.basis: Republican leaders tried to force through a five-year extension just after midnight on Friday, but while four Democrats voted in favor of the measure, twelve Republicans voted against it, sending the measure down to a loss by 20 votes.

events.title: Supreme Court reverses D.C. Court of Appeals in District of Columbia v. R.W., Fourth Amendment stop-and-frisk case
events.summary: The Supreme Court granted certiorari, reversed the District of Columbia Court of Appeals, and remanded the case. The lower court had held that Officer Vanterpool lacked reasonable articulable suspicion to stop R.W., a minor, at 2:00 a.m. in a parking lot after observing two companions flee from a vehicle and R.W. backing out with a car door open. The Supreme Court held that the officer had reasonable suspicion based on the totality of circumstances—the late-night dispatch call, the companions' unprovoked flight, and R.W.'s suspicious driving behavior—and reversed the suppression of evidence. Justice Jackson dissented, arguing the lower court correctly applied Fourth Amendment doctrine and that Supreme Court intervention was unwarranted.
events.why_relevant: This decision narrows Fourth Amendment protections by permitting police stops based on a lower threshold of suspicion and by reversing a lower court's protection of a minor's constitutional rights, affecting police power and individual liberty.
events.basis: The petition for certiorari and R. W.'s motion to proceed in forma pauperis are granted, the judgment of the District of Columbia Court of Appeals is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

events.title: House reauthorized Section 702 FISA surveillance powers for three years
events.summary: The House of Representatives passed a three-year reauthorization of Section 702 of FISA on Wednesday by a vote of 235–191. The program permits U.S. intelligence agencies to intercept communications of foreign nationals abroad without a warrant, but data of Americans communicating with those targets is swept up incidentally, and the FBI can search that data without a court order. Civil liberties advocates have sought a warrant requirement for nearly two decades, which was not included in the bill.
